title: CamelCase
directAnswer: In camelCase the first word starts lowercase and every later word begins with an uppercase letter. So the number of words equals the number of uppercase letters plus one. Scan once, count uppercase characters, return count + 1. O(n) time, O(1) space.

rules: Each new word (after the first) is signalled by **exactly one** uppercase letter — so uppercase letters and word-boundaries are in bijection.
Start the count at **1** for the leading lowercase word, then add one per uppercase letter.
Empty string is a special case: there are **zero** words, not one — guard for it if the constraints allow empty input.
Detect uppercase with `Character.isUpperCase(c)` / `c.isupper()`, not an ASCII range you might get wrong.
You never split the string — splitting allocates; counting does not.
whenToUse: Tokens are delimited by a case change rather than a separator character
You only need the count of tokens, not the tokens themselves
The first token is special (no leading delimiter) so you seed the count at 1
A single linear scan over characters suffices
antiSignals: Words are separated by spaces or punctuation → split on the delimiter instead
You must return the actual words → you build a list, not a counter
Mixed conventions (snake_case + camelCase) appear → counting uppercase alone is wrong
PascalCase where the first word is also capitalised → the +1 seed changes
remember.takeaway: When token boundaries are marked by a property of a single character (a case change), counting that property and adjusting for the first token gives the count in one pass — far cheaper than splitting into substrings.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you spot the bijection between uppercase letters and word boundaries, avoiding an unnecessary split into substrings just to call size().
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Splitting the string with a regex on case changes and counting the parts — correct but allocates a list and is easy to get wrong on edge cases like a leading capital.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the invariant out loud: 'first word has no marker, every other word starts with exactly one uppercase, so words = uppercase + 1', and call out the empty-string exception.

problemStatement:
A word in CamelCase notation starts with a lowercase letter; the start of each subsequent word is marked by an uppercase letter. For example, `oneTwoThree` has three words.

Given a camelCase string `s`, return the **number of words** it contains.
constraints: s contains only English letters (a–z, A–Z)
The first character is lowercase (standard camelCase, not PascalCase)
understanding: camelCase glues words together and uses capitalisation as the only delimiter. The first word is lowercase and unmarked; each later word announces itself with a single capital letter. Counting words therefore reduces to counting capitals and adding one for that unmarked first word.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the first letter guaranteed lowercase (camelCase) or could it be uppercase (PascalCase)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Standard camelCase starts lowercase, so the +1 accounts for that first word. If PascalCase were allowed, the leading capital would be over-counted and you'd return uppercase count directly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the string contain digits or symbols?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The classic prompt is letters only. If digits could start words you'd need a richer boundary rule, but for this problem only case changes matter.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the input be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If allowed, empty means zero words — not one. Guard for length 0 before returning count + 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the count or the list of words?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the count, which is exactly why we can avoid building any substrings.

approaches.name: Split on Case Changes (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show you can tokenise, then note it allocates a list you immediately discard.
hints: You could insert a delimiter before every uppercase letter, then split into tokens and count them.
A regex like splitting before each capital, or a manual builder that adds a space before uppercase, gives you the words.
It works, but you allocate an array of substrings only to read its length — can the count come for free?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the delimited string and splitting both touch every character, so O(n) time, and the resulting list of words plus the rebuilt string cost O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The direct approach tokenises the string into the actual words, then returns how many there are. You walk the input, start a new token whenever you hit an uppercase letter, collect the tokens, and report the size.

**Why it is correct.** A case change is the only word boundary in camelCase, so cutting at every uppercase letter recovers exactly the original words. The number of tokens is the answer.

**Why it is heavier than needed.** To get a single integer you allocated a whole list of substrings (and possibly a rebuilt, space-separated copy of the input). That is `O(n)` extra memory and a lot of moving parts — regex edge cases, leading-empty-token handling, and so on. Since the question only asks *how many* words, you never actually need the words themselves.

**The takeaway.** Producing the tokens answers a harder question than was asked. Recognising that 'count of words' is fully captured by 'count of boundary markers' lets you drop the allocation entirely.
approaches.insight: If a regex split produces a leading empty token (e.g. when the string starts with a capital in PascalCase), your count is off by one — exactly the kind of edge case the counting approach sidesteps.

approaches.name: Count Uppercase Letters + 1 (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Say 'each capital starts a new word, plus one for the leading lowercase word'.
hints: Every word after the first begins with exactly one uppercase letter. What does that say about the relationship between capitals and words?
Capitals and 'new word' events are in one-to-one correspondence. The first word has no capital, so seed your count at 1.
Scan once, add 1 for every uppercase letter, return the running total. No splitting, no extra memory.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n characters with a constant-time uppercase test each → O(n) time. Only an integer counter is kept → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Initialise a word counter to `1` and increment it by one for every uppercase letter you encounter. Return the counter.

**Why the seed is 1.** camelCase always opens with a lowercase word that carries no marker. That first word exists regardless of how many capitals follow, so it is counted up front. If you seeded at `0`, an all-lowercase string like `"hello"` would wrongly return `0` instead of `1`.

**Why each capital adds exactly one word.** The convention guarantees that a new word begins precisely at an uppercase letter, and a word starts with a *single* capital — the rest of the word is lowercase. So there is a clean bijection: one uppercase letter ⇔ one new word boundary. Summing the boundaries and adding the unmarked first word gives `uppercase_count + 1`.

**Why this beats splitting.** You answer the exact question asked — *how many* words — without ever materialising the words. There is no token list, no regex, no leading-empty-token trap. The only state is one integer, so the space is constant and the logic has almost no surface area for bugs.

**The one exception to remember.** An empty string has zero words, but `uppercase_count + 1` would return `1`. Guard for empty input first when the constraints permit it, then apply the formula.
approaches.insight: The trick is recognising the bijection: in camelCase, 'number of word boundaries' literally equals 'number of uppercase letters'. Once boundaries map to a countable per-character property, you collapse a tokenising problem into a single counting loop.

dryRun.intro: Seed at 1 for 'save'; bump on every capital. No tokens built.

java.explanation: Empty string has zero words — the +1 formula would wrongly return 1 without this guard.
Seed for the leading lowercase word that carries no uppercase marker.
Each capital marks the start of a new word — locale-safe uppercase test.
One capital ⇔ one new word boundary.

python.explanation: Empty input → zero words, bypassing the +1.

python.line: return 1 + sum(1 for c in s if c.isupper())
python.explanation: One for the first word, plus one per uppercase letter — the whole algorithm in one line.

pitfalls: Seeding the count at 0 — an all-lowercase string then returns 0 instead of 1.
Forgetting the empty-string guard — the formula returns 1 for no words.
Assuming PascalCase: a leading capital would be over-counted by the +1.

commonMistakes: Returning the uppercase count without the +1 for the first word.
Splitting into tokens and miscounting because of a leading empty token.
Treating PascalCase like camelCase — the leading capital breaks the +1 assumption.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the +1 for the first word
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The first word has no uppercase marker, so counting only capitals undercounts by one for every camelCase string.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one from a leading empty token
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Splitting before each capital on a PascalCase string yields an empty first token, inflating the count by one.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return 1 + sum(1 for c in s if c.isupper())

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning 1 for an empty string
commonMistakesDetailed.why: An empty input contains zero words, but the +1 formula returns 1 unless you guard for emptiness first.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return 1 + sum(1 for c in s if c.isupper())

patternNote: Boundary-marker counting. When tokens are delimited by a per-character property (here, an uppercase letter) and you only need the count, tally that property in one pass and adjust for the unmarked first token instead of splitting into substrings.
